name: Pretectal area
summary: A group of small nuclei at the junction of the midbrain and diencephalon, just in front of the superior colliculus and beside the posterior commissure. They are the central relay of the pupillary light reflex: each receives retinal fibers from both eyes via the optic tract and brachium of the superior colliculus and projects to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei, partly through the posterior commissure. This bilateral wiring is why light in one eye constricts both pupils and why a pretectal lesion produces light-near dissociation rather than blindness.

anatomy.location: Rostral to the superior colliculus at the level of the posterior commissure, lateral to the aqueduct's upper end, between the tectum and the pulvinar.

function: Afferent center of the pupillary light reflex; contributes to the accommodation reflex and to vertical gaze through the posterior commissure and interstitial nucleus of Cajal.

bestView.label: junction of the tectum and thalamus at the posterior commissure
rostral to the superior colliculus beneath the pineal

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; the region is the dorsal midbrain–diencephalic junction just below the pineal and behind the third ventricle.

pathology.finding: Pineal tumor, tectal glioma, hydrocephalus or infarct compressing or involving the posterior commissure and pretectum.
Imaging usually normal; the lesion is in the pretectal light-reflex fibers (classically neurosyphilis).

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial T2 of the pineal region; serology for syphilis when pupils dissociate

lesionEffects.deficit: Light-near dissociation: pupils react to near but not to light
lesionEffects.mechanism: Interruption of the light reflex arc while the near reflex reaches Edinger–Westphal by a more ventral route

lesionEffects.deficit: Bilateral mid-dilated pupils with poor light reaction plus up-gaze palsy
Relative afferent pupillary defect is NOT produced
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lesions here are usually bilateral; RAPD needs an asymmetric afferent lesion in front of the pretectum

examination: Pupil reaction to light then to a near target
Swinging flashlight test to exclude an afferent (optic nerve) cause
pearls: Light-near dissociation localizes to the pretectum or the ciliary ganglion; up-gaze palsy alongside it makes it the dorsal midbrain
Argyll Robertson pupils are small and irregular; Adie pupils are large and slow
